text:
maria: Heads-up — I'm trying to repro the KV-cache perf regression and want to capture an nsys trace that shows kernel timelines + NVTX regions + OS runtime events. Any recommended CLI flags?

kevin: For that combo I usually do: `nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt -o kvtrace` to get kernels, NVTX markers, and OS runtime info.

zach: +1. Add `--sample=cpu` if you want CPU stack sampling (helps find CPU-side hotspots like batching loops). It does add overhead though.

maria: How do you limit capture time? I don't want a 10GB file.

natalie: Use `--duration-ms` or the `--timeout` option depending on your nsys version. E.g. `--duration-ms=5000` for a 5s capture, or wrap with `nsys profile -o out --trace=... --duration-ms=5000 -- <cmd>`

kevin: Another pattern: instrument the critical region with NVTX push/pop in runtime, then run `nsys profile --capture-range=nvtx --capture-range-start=region:start --capture-range-end=region:end ...` That narrows the capture to only the NVTX-scoped window and keeps files small.

zach: If you can't change code, use `--capture=process` + `--capture-children` and start/stop the model worker around the run.

perf-bot: Reminder: enabling `osrt` increases detail for threads and syscalls, but it can blow up file size. Prefer it for short, targeted captures.

maria: What's the sampling config you all use? I've seen `--sample=cpu` vs `--sample=none`. Any rate knobs?

kevin: You can control sampling granularity with `--sample-interval` or `--sample=cpu --sample-interval=1000` (check your nsys manpage for exact flag name/version). Lower interval -> more samples -> more overhead. For initial triage I set interval to 1000-5000us.

natalie: Also consider `--trace=cuda,cublas,osrt,nvtx` if you suspect cuBLAS kernels (matmuls) are involved. cublas traces show library launches.

zach: Practical tips: 1) Run a baseline (no quant) and the regression build with identical input sequences. 2) Use `nsys stats` to quickly compare kernel time per-kernel. 3) Use the timeline in UI to spot long gaps or very frequent tiny kernels (bad for batching).

maria: Any gotchas for KV-cache (lots of small KV cache reads) traces?

kevin: Small kernels show up as tons of tiny launches. In timeline they appear as a dense stack of short bars. If you see GPU utilization low but lots of PCIe/CUDA API calls on CPU thread, the issue might be split launches or CPU-side batching.

natalie: If you suspect kernel selection logic doing extra CPU work, add NVTX markers around the selection/batching code paths so they appear alongside kernels. That helps correlate which policy path triggered which kernel.

zach: When comparing runs, export per-kernel aggregated metrics: `nsys stats -r cuda -f csv report.qdrep` and diff the tables. Look for large changes in avg duration or launch counts.

maria: Thanks — one more: any CLI to reduce captured syscalls/overhead? I only need kernels + nvtx, not full syscall tracing.

kevin: Drop `osrt` if you don't need syscalls/thread scheduling. `--trace=cuda,nvtx` is much lighter. If you need some OS info but not full, there's limited granularity — prefer short captures with `osrt` rather than long ones.

perf-bot: Quick checklist before running: 1) Rebuild with debug NVTX if possible. 2) Disable other noisy processes (X server on dev box). 3) Run warmup iterations to stabilize caches. 4) Use capture-range (NVTX) to limit size.

maria: Perfect. I'll run two captures tonight: 5s with `--trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt` (targeted NVTX window) and a lighter 10s `--trace=cuda,nvtx` for longer behavior. Will post qdrep after upload.

kevin: If you share the qdrep I can run `nsys stats` and a quick kernel-aggregate diff.

zach: FYI: when you open the qdrep in the UI, enable the "GPU Context" lane and show kernel correlations. That usually exposes blocked kernels waiting on memcpy or stream syncs.

maria: Thanks team — starting now. I'll ping with links. :rocket:
